facts.one_liner: Dublin Bridge Street pub with a brick façade, gold sign, and claim as Ireland’s oldest hostelry.
facts.why_go: The Brazen Head sits on Lower Bridge Street beside Father Matthew Bridge, where an inn has long claimed roots back to 1198; the present coaching-inn fabric is largely mid-18th century (c. 1754). The photo matches the weathered brick exterior: crenellated parapet, barred windows, hanging baskets, and the black-and-gold “The Brazen Head” board above a plaque advertising Ireland’s oldest pub. Barrels often sit on the pavement outside; inside, the rooms still run as a gastrobar with nightly traditional music.
facts.best_time: Weekday early afternoon for a quieter exterior photo and seat; evenings bring live traditional music (typically from about 9pm) and fuller rooms. Sunday afternoon sessions are a local favourite.
facts.how_to_get_there: 20 Lower Bridge Street, Dublin 8 (D08 WC64), a short walk west of Christ Church Cathedral and south of the Liffey. LUAS Red Line to Four Courts or Smithfield; buses along the quays and Bridge Street; about 15–20 minutes’ walk from Temple Bar.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN as of 2025–2026 (official site: daily from 12pm to late; food until 9pm). Cash/card as posted; groups under 8 generally walk in without reservations. Busy tourist landmark—arrive early if you want a table near the music room.

facts.one_liner: Fleet Street alley pub rebuilt after the Great Fire—sign reads Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, Rebuilt 1667.
facts.why_go: Tucked off Fleet Street in Wine Office Court, this Samuel Smith’s house is one of the City’s best-known historic pubs: a maze of panelled rooms rebuilt after the Great Fire and famous with literary regulars from Dr Johnson’s circle to Dickens. The photo shows the narrow stone alley approach—the circular hanging sign announcing “Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese REBUILT 1667,” lantern, and steps down into the bars. Come for the subterranean feel of the courts rather than a street-front terrace.
facts.best_time: Midweek mid-afternoon is usually calmer than lunch or after-work peaks; evenings and weekends fill the interconnecting rooms quickly.
facts.how_to_get_there: 145 Fleet Street, London EC4A 2BP; entrance via Wine Office Court off Fleet Street. Closest Tube: Blackfriars, Temple, or Chancery Lane; City Thameslink / Blackfriars also nearby.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN as of 2025–2026 (official hours Mon–Sat 12–23:00, Sun 12–22:30). Samuel Smith’s beers only; no wheelchair access (steep historic layout). No smoking/drinking in the alley—follow posted notices.

facts.one_liner: Munich’s state beer palace on Platzl—white Neo-Renaissance façade with the crowned blue HB monogram.
facts.why_go: Staatliches Hofbräuhaus am Platzl began as Duke Wilhelm V’s court brewery in 1589; King Ludwig I opened it to the public in 1828, and the present tavern building is Max Littmann’s 1896–97 Neo-Renaissance rebuild (post-war reconstruction finished by 1958). The photo captures the Platzl exterior: pale façade, ornate bay/erker, arched ground-floor entrance, and the large blue crowned “HB” with “Hofbräuhaus” script. Inside, the Schwemme seats about a thousand at long tables with daily Bavarian music; brewing itself moved away long ago (now Riem).
facts.best_time: Late morning opening or mid-afternoon on weekdays for a less crowded hall; summer evenings and weekends in the Altstadt are busiest. Wirtsgarten is seasonal.
facts.how_to_get_there: Platzl 9, 80331 Munich. S-Bahn/U-Bahn to Marienplatz or Isartor; about a 5–7 minute walk through the Old Town. Tram Nationaltheater also nearby.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN daily ~11:00–00:00 as of 2025–2026 (kitchen earlier; last drinks ~23:30). No reservation needed for the Schwemme—share tables; groups of 4+ can book other rooms. Free entry during opening hours; Maßkrug lockers are for regulars only.

facts.one_liner: Munich’s oldest beer garden—enter under chestnuts through the Arnulfstraße 52 gateway.
facts.why_go: Augustiner-Keller on Arnulfstraße is Munich’s oldest beer garden: the site appears on an 1812 city map, and the outdoor layout has kept much the same look since the 1890s, with more than 100 chestnut trees shading about 5,000 seats. The photo is the street gateway—stone pillars, green wooden pergola, Arnulfstr. 52 sign, and the path rising into the garden—not the indoor Keller alone. Augustiner Edelstoff is poured from wooden barrels; self-service and waiter areas sit under the trees beside Circus Krone.
facts.best_time: Warm, dry afternoons April–September when the garden is officially open (seasonal; weather-dependent). Weekday early evening beats peak weekend crush.
facts.how_to_get_there: Arnulfstraße 52, 80335 Munich, west of the Hauptbahnhof toward Circus Krone. S-Bahn/U-Bahn Hauptbahnhof then ~10-minute walk; tram/bus along Arnulfstraße.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN as of 2025–2026: beer garden typically 11:00–midnight when weather and demand allow (kitchen earlier); restaurant/terraces keep longer winter hours—check the day’s status on augustinerkeller.de. Bring your own snack for the self-service area if you follow local custom; no prices listed here.

facts.one_liner: Bamberg’s Schlenkerla — historic Heller brewery tavern tapping Aecht Schlenkerla Rauchbier.
facts.why_go: Schlenkerla on Dominikanerstraße 6 is the historic brewery tavern of Heller-Bräu Trum in Bamberg’s old town, first mentioned as the House of the Blue Lion in 1405 and still run by the Trum family. The Commons photo shows the timber-framed façade and hanging signs of the Ausschank where Aecht Schlenkerla Rauchbier (smoked beer) is still drawn from wooden barrels. Bamberg’s UNESCO old town sits around the Domberg above; the tavern is a short walk downhill from the cathedral. Morning pint service starts early; the Dominikanerhof beer garden opens weather permitting in warmer months.
facts.best_time: Year-round for the tavern (daily hours). Beer garden typically Easter to early October when weather allows. Expect Christmas/New Year closures — check schlenkerla.de for holiday dates.
facts.how_to_get_there: Dominikanerstraße 6, 96049 Bamberg. Train to Bamberg station, then walk (~15–20 min) into the Altstadt toward Dominikanerstraße below the Dom, or use local buses. Table reservations advised for peak evenings.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN daily roughly 9:30–23:30; kitchen ~11:00–22:00 (confirm on schlenkerla.de). Smoked beer tastes intensely of beechwood at first sip — the house says keep going.

facts.why_go: McSorley’s Old Ale House at 15 East 7th Street bills itself as New York’s oldest continuously operated saloon (est. 1854), with sawdust floors, history-patched walls, and a famously short ale menu. The photo is the classic storefront: “McSORLEY’S OLD ALE HOUSE / ESTABLISHED 1854” board, multi-pane windows with gold slogans, open doorway, and green sidewalk barrels. facts.one_liner: Victorian Dublin pub on South Great George’s—ruby-red front, striped awnings, and gold script sign.
facts.why_go: The Long Hall at 51 South Great George’s Street has traded as a public house since 1766; Patrick Dolan’s 1879–1881 refit created the affluent Victorian interior of mahogany, mirrors, and clocks that Visit Dublin still highlights. The photo is the narrow street façade: deep red ground floor, “The Long Hall” in gold script with the number 51, red-and-white striped awnings on every floor, and twin doors flanking a central window. Locals and visitors still use it as a classic city-centre pint stop rather than a theme-park bar.
facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons for a calmer stand at the bar; Friday–Saturday evenings fill quickly. Daylight helps for the striped-awning exterior shot.
facts.how_to_get_there: 51 South Great George’s Street, Dublin 2 (D02 DV74), between Dame Street and Aungier Street, near Dublin Castle. LUAS Green Line to Trinity or St Stephen’s Green; many city buses along George’s Street.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN as of 2025–2026 (recent tourism and local listings show regular daytime–evening hours; confirm by phone +353 1 475 1590 before late visits). Compact Victorian rooms—standing room common at peak.

facts.one_liner: Prague brewery-pub brewing since 1499—street clock spelling PIVOVAR U FLEKŮ under a golden bear.
facts.why_go: U Fleků on Křemencova is among Central Europe’s longest continuously brewing houses: written records begin in 1499 with maltster Vít Skřemenec, and the house still pours its house Flekovský dark lager (13°) with Old Bohemian food across multiple historic halls and a garden. The photo focuses on the ornate street clock—black ironwork, letters circling “PIVOVAR U FLEKŮ,” golden bear finial, and “Dej Bůh štěstí” on the side panel—mounted on the ochre façade. Prague City Tourism lists it as a landmark brewery-restaurant rather than a quiet neighbourhood bar.
facts.best_time: Late morning or early afternoon before tour groups peak; evenings and weekends are lively. Museum and cabaret need advance booking.
facts.how_to_get_there: Křemencova 11, Prague 1 (New Town / near Národní). Metro B to Národní třída; tram to Národní divadlo or Karlovo náměstí; short walk into Křemencova.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN daily 10:00–23:00 as of 2025–2026 per Prague City Tourism and the brewery (typically closed 24 Dec). Reservations recommended for halls; expect a tourist-heavy courtyard. Brewery museum and weekend cabaret are separate, bookable experiences.

facts.one_liner: Leipzig cellar tavern since 1525—Fraktur Schriftzug marks Goethe’s Faust haunt in Mädler-Passage.
facts.why_go: Auerbachs Keller began as physician Heinrich Stromer von Auerbach’s student wine cellar in 1525 beneath what is now Mädler-Passage. Goethe studied in Leipzig from 1765 and drew on the cellar’s Faust barrel-ride paintings (1625) for the Auerbachs Keller scene in Faust; bronze Faust/Mephisto figures still stand on the passage stairs. The photo is the exterior Schriftzug—dark Fraktur metal letters “Auerbachs / Keller” on a pale wall—so the visit starts at that named entrance before descending to Großer Keller, historic Weinstuben, and Mephisto Bar.
facts.best_time: Weekday lunch or early evening; Advent weekends are especially busy. Book for Großer Keller and Faust-themed tours.
facts.how_to_get_there: Mädler-Passage, Grimmaische Straße 2–4, 04109 Leipzig (city centre). Tram/S-Bahn to Augustusplatz or Markt; short walk into the passage.
facts.good_to_know: OPEN as of 2025–2026: Großer Keller typically Mon/Thu/Sun 12–22, Tue–Wed 17–22, Fri–Sat 12–23; Mephisto Bar has separate (often longer) hours—confirm on auerbachs-keller-leipzig.de. Historic wine rooms often need groups or guided programmes. 500th-anniversary programming has run in the mid-2020s.

facts.one_liner: London’s last galleried coaching inn—white timber galleries above a cobbled Southwark courtyard.
facts.why_go: The George Inn on Borough High Street is London’s last remaining galleried coaching inn: a National Trust property leased to Greene King, rebuilt after the 1676 Southwark fire and still opening onto a cobbled yard. The photo shows the white façade with black framing, two tiers of open wooden galleries, hanging baskets, St George hanging sign, and picnic tables in the courtyard—exactly the coaching-inn silhouette visitors come to see. Dickens knew the site (mentioned in Little Dorrit); Borough Market and London Bridge sit minutes away.
facts.best_time: Dry midday or late afternoon for courtyard seating and clear gallery photos; Friday–Saturday evenings and market days are busiest. Book ahead for indoor meals.
facts.how_to_get_there: The George Inn Yard, 75–77 Borough High Street, Southwark, London SE1 1NH. Tube/rail: London Bridge (Northern, Jubilee, National Rail); short walk south along Borough High Street.

The pink-elephant façade on the narrow alley marks the bar named after Huyghe’s Delirium Tremens; Jeanneke Pis stands nearby. Writer Bohumil Hrabal made it famous in his stories; on 11 January 1994 President Václav Havel brought Bill Clinton (and Madeleine Albright) here for Pilsner Urquell. facts.why_go: Sean’s Bar faces Main Street in Athlone beside the Shannon and Athlone Castle—the low street façade captured in a 2025 Commons photo. facts.best_time: Daytime for history displays and quieter pints; evenings for traditional music when scheduled. Closed Christmas Day.

facts.best_time: Evening absinthe service (city guide lists from 18:00 most days). Weeknights calmer than Friday–Saturday.
facts.how_to_get_there: Carrer de Sant Pau 65, 08001 Barcelona (Ciutat Vella / El Raval). Metro Liceu (L3) or Paral·lel; short walk from La Rambla into Sant Pau.

facts.one_liner: Gramercy corner tavern since 1864; claims continuous NYC bar/restaurant operation.
facts.why_go: Pete’s Tavern occupies the corner of East 18th Street and Irving Place in Gramercy, less than five minutes from Union Square—the street exterior in the photo. A drinking room opened here in 1864 (building 1851); as Healy’s Café it was a haunt of O. The house claims continuous operation through Prohibition as a florist-fronted speakeasy; the rosewood bar, tin ceiling, and tile floor remain signature fixtures.

facts.one_liner: Düsseldorf’s historic Altbier brewery-tavern in the old town.
facts.why_go: Zum Schiffchen in Düsseldorf’s Altstadt traces its history to 1628, making it one of the city’s oldest inns. Blue-aproned ‘Köbes’ waiters keep fresh glasses of Altbier coming until you put your coaster on top. Napoleon Bonaparte is said to have dined here in 1811.
facts.best_time: Year-round; summer for the outdoor tables, November–February for the Rhineland carnival season.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Hafenstraße in the Altstadt, a short walk from the Rhine promenade and Heinrich-Heine-Allee U-Bahn.
facts.good_to_know: Put your beer mat on your glass to stop refills. Hearty Rhineland dishes are served.

facts.one_liner: A rambling mountain pub above Dublin, famous for its ‘Hooley’ nights.
facts.why_go: High in the hamlet of Glencullen in the Dublin Mountains, Johnnie Fox’s claims to date from 1798 and to be one of Ireland’s highest pubs. Its rambling rooms are packed with old farm tools, signs and bric-a-brac, and its Hooley show combines dinner, traditional music and Irish dancing.
facts.best_time: Year-round; evenings for the Hooley show, fireside winter nights.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 30–40 minutes by car from Dublin city centre; the pub runs a shuttle bus for Hooley guests.
facts.good_to_know: Book the Hooley ahead. Mountain roads are narrow and winding.

facts.one_liner: The colonial bar at Raffles where the Singapore Sling was created.
facts.why_go: The Long Bar at Singapore’s Raffles Hotel is where bartender Ngiam Tong Boon created the Singapore Sling in the early 20th century. Inspired by Malayan plantation life, the bar has wooden fittings and rattan fans, and guests are encouraged to brush peanut shells onto the floor.
facts.best_time: Year-round (Singapore is hot all year); afternoons are calmest.
facts.how_to_get_there: In the Raffles Arcade on Beach Road, a short walk from City Hall or Esplanade MRT stations.
facts.good_to_know: Expect queues and premium prices. Smart-casual dress.

facts.one_liner: A Victorian gin palace of etched glass and painted ladies opposite the Old Bailey.
facts.why_go: The Viaduct Tavern on Newgate Street was built in 1869, the year Holborn Viaduct opened, and is one of London’s best-preserved Victorian gin palaces. Its interior has etched and gilded glass, a pressed-metal ceiling and large paintings of female figures. Stories link its cellars to the old Newgate Prison across the road.
facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons; it is busy after work.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Newgate Street, about 5 minutes’ walk from St Paul’s station.
facts.good_to_know: Ask staff about the cellars—sometimes shown to visitors.

facts.one_liner: Key West’s legendary Duval Street bar with Hemingway lore and live music.
facts.why_go: Sloppy Joe’s grew out of the bar run by Joe Russell, Ernest Hemingway’s friend and fishing partner in the 1930s, and moved to its current building at Duval and Greene streets in 1937. With open sides, ceiling fans and live music from midday, it is the centre of Key West nightlife and hosts the Hemingway Look-Alike Contest during Hemingway Days each July.
facts.best_time: December–April for dry, warm weather; July for Hemingway Days.
facts.how_to_get_there: At 201 Duval Street in Old Town Key West; Key West International Airport is about 15 minutes away.
facts.good_to_know: It is busy when cruise ships are in port. Hurricane season runs June–November.

facts.one_liner: Cunard’s flagship ocean liner, here gliding through a Norwegian fjord, with a classic British pub on board.
facts.why_go: Queen Mary 2 has been Cunard’s flagship since 2004 and is the only ship built as an ocean liner still in service, sailing regular transatlantic crossings between Southampton and New York as well as cruises and an annual world voyage. On board, the Golden Lion is a traditional British pub with pub lunches, quizzes and live music—perfect between days at sea, ballroom evenings and the planetarium.
facts.best_time: Transatlantic crossings run mainly from spring to autumn; summer cruises often visit the Norwegian fjords.
facts.how_to_get_there: Most voyages start at Southampton (about 80 minutes by train from London Waterloo) or Brooklyn Cruise Terminal in New York.
facts.good_to_know: A crossing takes about seven nights. Some evenings have dress codes; check Cunard’s guidance.
